source.title: Revisiting Video Quality Assessment from the Perspective of Generalization
source.authors: Xin-Li Yue; Jian-Hui Sun; Liangchao Yao; Fan Xia; Yuetang Deng; Tianyi Wang; Lei Li; Feng-Yun Rao; Jing Lv; Qian Wang; Ling-Chen Zhao

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures training–test generalization gaps and loss-landscape smoothness in video quality assessment, and finds counterexamples to a simple smoothness–gap relationship: augmentation and random weight perturbation can reduce the gap without improving test performance. It does not test the claim versions about natural-label classification, architecture, optimizer, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: Results bear on the claim's generalization-gap subject, but not on V1–V8 as defined: the paper studies quality-assessment correlation metrics on video datasets and weight-loss landscapes. It reports its own VQA results in the rows below. Tables 6–13 include comparisons and benchmark results that do not directly test the listed claim versions, so they are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests relationships between filter-normalized loss-landscape curves and correlation-based generalization gaps in video quality regression, plus regularization interventions. None measures V1–V8. In particular, it does not evaluate V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance before training error rises, comparable low-loss convolutional networks, or rankings against norm and margin measures. Its counterexamples concern test performance, whereas V7 concerns the training–test gap.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' broad conclusion: smoother VQA loss landscapes accompany smaller training–test gaps, and suitably configured AWP improves generalization across multiple datasets and methods. They also emphasize that smoothing and reducing the gap alone need not improve test performance. Their broad AWP conclusion does not imply improvement at every magnitude or on every metric.
record.recipe_differences: Video quality regression rather than classification; correlation metrics (SRCC and PLCC) and loss-landscape visualization; evaluates L2 regularization, augmentation, RWP and AWP. The authors cite classification work on landscape/generalization but do not reproduce the catalog's original methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset (KoNViD-1k versus YouTubeUGC), intervention type (L2, augmentation, RWP, AWP), and perturbation magnitude affect test performance and/or generalization gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Across training epochs and three VQA methods, sharper filter-normalized loss-landscape curves accompany larger training–test correlation gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Qualitative filter-normalized landscape sharpness correlates with correlation-based generalization gaps in the tested VQA models.

fits_no_version.finding: Augmentation and large random weight perturbations reduce correlation gaps without consistent improvements in test correlation; RWP at 0.01 substantially lowers test performance on both datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A smaller correlation gap and smoother landscape do not ensure improved held-out quality prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: AWP improves test SRCC at all three smaller magnitudes on KoNViD-1k, but excessive perturbation hurts. On YouTubeUGC, 0.001 and 0.00001 improve SRCC, while 0.0001 lowers it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AWP's benefit for VQA depends on perturbation magnitude and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing L2 regularization produces nearly overlapping landscape curves and limited performance changes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: L2 regularization has limited influence on landscape smoothness in these VQA experiments.

record.problems: The evidence is specific to VQA regression on the reported datasets and uses correlation metrics rather than classification error. Some landscape comparisons are figure-only; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper notes reproduced SAMA results differed significantly from the original SAMA paper.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 6–9 report model benchmark/cross-dataset comparisons and perturbation ablations, but these do not report the claim versions' classification behaviors; Table 8 concerns IQA. PLCC values alongside extracted SRCC conditions, and other benchmark method rows, were omitted to keep rows focused on the generalization-gap and landscape findings.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out performance compared with natural-label classification.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout addition, excessive dropout, small-data regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.

Magnitude-aware sharpness measured by perturbation tolerance before training error rises, its correlation with error gaps among comparable low-loss convolutional networks, and comparison with norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because no row measures a listed version. This does not dispute the study's VQA findings. Several extracted values confused adjacent regularization settings or RWP with AWP. Missing is empty because no unrecorded result tests V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: random-label memorization and natural-label generalization in classification
width sweep beyond interpolation in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks
convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers
adaptive optimizers versus SGD on classification and language benchmarks
large-batch versus small-batch training under fixed epoch budgets
dropout effects and removal of dropout/weight decay
magnitude-aware sharpness comparison against norm- and margin-based measures
removal of memorized training examples and resulting test-accuracy change
